topic: System design approach & app architecture on Android and iOS

questions.question: You are asked to "design an offline-capable notes app for Android and iOS." What should you do in the first few minutes?
options: Start with the class diagram for the notes repository and its data sources
Pick Room or SQLDelight first, so the local data layer is settled early on
Clarify scope: core features, offline and sync needs, scale and platforms
Draw the backend database schema first, since the client depends on it
questions.explanation: Requirements and constraints decide almost every later choice, such as how conflicts are resolved and what is cached. Interviewers look for this framing before any boxes are drawn. Jumping to a library or class diagram risks designing the wrong system in detail.

questions.question: In a layered architecture, the domain layer may import Android's `Context` as long as it is injected rather than created there.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The domain layer should not depend on any platform framework, so it stays testable on the plain JVM and shareable, for example through Kotlin Multiplatform. Anything that needs Context belongs in the data or platform layer behind an interface the domain defines.

questions.question: Feature module `:checkout` must open a screen in `:profile`, and `:profile` must open one in `:checkout`. How do you avoid a dependency cycle?
options: Merge both features into one shared `:features` module to remove the cycle
Make `:checkout` depend on `:profile`, and pass callbacks back the other way
Load the other module's screens by class name at runtime using reflection
Depend only on small API or navigation contract modules; wire them in `:app`
questions.explanation: Splitting each feature into an API contract and an implementation lets features depend on contracts only, while the app module, which sees everything, binds implementations. Merging gives up the build-time and ownership benefits, and reflection loses compile-time safety and needs keep rules. One-way dependencies with callbacks only work until the next feature needs the reverse link.

questions.question: An iOS team uses The Composable Architecture (TCA). Which Android pattern is it closest to?
options: Classic MVC, with view controllers owning and mutating the screen's state
MVI-style unidirectional flow: a store, a reducer for actions, effects for async
MVP, where a presenter calls methods on a passive view interface
Plain MVVM with two-way data binding between the view and its model
questions.explanation: TCA has a Store holding state, a reducer that handles actions and returns effects, and dependencies injected for testing, which is MVI in Swift form. Plain MVVM on iOS usually means an `@Observable` or ObservableObject view model with methods. MVP and two-way binding do not have the single reducer at the centre.

questions.question: Work started in SwiftUI's `.task { }` modifier is cancelled automatically when the view disappears, much like a `LaunchedEffect` leaving composition.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. `.task` ties an async task to the view's lifetime and cancels it on disappear, and `.task(id:)` restarts it when the id changes, much like a LaunchedEffect key. Unstructured `Task { }` created elsewhere is not cancelled automatically and must be stored and cancelled by hand.

questions.question: In Swift 6 language mode, a `@MainActor` view model passes an instance of a non-Sendable class into a `Task.detached` closure. What happens?
options: A compile-time error: data-race checking rejects the non-Sendable value
A runtime crash the first time both tasks touch the shared object
Nothing happens; Swift copies class instances when they cross actors
Only a warning, because data-race diagnostics are always advisory in Swift
questions.explanation: Swift 6 language mode enforces Sendable checking as errors, so sending a non-Sendable reference into a detached task does not compile. That is a real difference from Kotlin coroutines, where sharing mutable state across dispatchers compiles and races at runtime. Classes are reference types and are never implicitly copied.

questions.question: Which statements about local persistence on the two platforms are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Core Data managed objects can be passed freely between threads and contexts
Room rejects queries on the main thread unless you explicitly allow them
Room checks SQL queries against the schema at compile time
SwiftData builds on Core Data's persistence stack and declares models with the `@Model` macro
questions.explanation: Room validates queries during the build, and by default throws if you query on the main thread. SwiftData is Apple's Swift-first layer over Core Data's storage, using macros instead of model editor files. Core Data objects belong to their context's queue, so passing them across threads is a classic crash; pass object IDs instead.

questions.question: What is the closest SwiftUI equivalent of `var expanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }` inside a composable?
options: `@Binding var expanded: Bool`
`@Environment(\.expanded) var expanded`
`@State private var expanded = false`
`static var expanded = false`
questions.explanation: `@State` is view-local state owned by SwiftUI that survives body re-evaluation and triggers updates, like `remember { mutableStateOf() }`. `@Binding` is a reference to state owned by a parent, closer to passing a value and a callback down. Environment values are closer to CompositionLocals.

questions.question: A chat app must show new messages instantly while open and notify the user when it is in the background, on both platforms. Which design fits?
options: Keep a WebSocket open at all times, including while the app is in the background
Poll the server every 5 seconds, both in the foreground and in the background
Use only push notifications, even while the chat screen itself is open
A WebSocket in the foreground; FCM or APNs push in the background
questions.explanation: Both operating systems suspend or limit background apps, so a socket will not stay alive reliably there, while push is designed for that case. In the foreground, a socket gives low-latency delivery and typing indicators that push cannot match. Polling wastes battery and is still delayed.

questions.question: Which platform differences should shape a cross-platform mobile design? Select all that apply.
options: iOS apps can keep a WebSocket open indefinitely in the background if the user allows notifications
Push goes through APNs on iOS and typically FCM on Android, with different payload and delivery behaviour
Android no longer restricts background work, so it can sync continuously
iOS background execution is more limited, scheduled through BGTaskScheduler, while Android has WorkManager for deferrable work
questions.explanation: Background work and push differ enough that sync and notification flows often need per-platform designs behind a shared interface. Notification permission does not keep a backgrounded iOS app running. Android restricts background work through Doze, App Standby and background execution limits, so continuous sync is not an option either.
